title: Pride And Prejudice: Chapter XX
enhanced_title: Chapter Twenty: The Rejection and Its Aftermath
author: Jane Austen
description: In Chapter 20 of Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth Bennet's rejection of Mr. Collins's marriage proposal creates significant family turmoil. Mr. Collins, convinced Elizabeth's refusal stems from feminine modesty, must be disabused of this notion by Mrs. Bennet, who desperately seeks to salvage the match. Mr. Bennet intervenes with characteristic wit, offering Elizabeth an ironic choice between her parents' favor. Despite Mrs. Bennet's continued pressure and emotional appeals, Elizabeth remains steadfast. Mr. Collins, nursing wounded pride but no real affection, eventually withdraws his suit with formal resignation. The chapter satirizes the mercenary concerns of marriage and the comic dynamics of the Bennet household.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Collins's inability to comprehend Elizabeth's genuine refusal demonstrates his profound self-delusion and the dangerous irony of interpreting a woman's clear 'no' as coquettish encouragement. His character embodies how social conventions around courtship can be weaponized to dismiss female agency. Austen makes plain that his attachment was never real: his regard for her was quite imaginary, and wounded pride rather than wounded feeling is all he suffers.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
His regard for her was quite imaginary; and the possibility of her
deserving her mother’s reproach prevented his feeling any regret.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mrs. Bennet's frantic reaction reveals the desperate economic anxiety driving her maternal pressure. Her contradictory characterization of Elizabeth—simultaneously 'headstrong, foolish' yet 'good-natured'—shows how mothers in this society must perform rhetorical gymnastics to make their daughters marriageable while explaining away resistance. The speed of her exit from Mr. Collins is itself comic: she would not give him time to reply, but hurrying instantly to her husband, called out, as she entered the library.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
She would not give him time to reply, but hurrying instantly to her
husband, called out, as she entered the library,--

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Bennet's intervention represents the moral center of the chapter, using irony as a weapon against social coercion. His famous declaration subverts patriarchal expectations by supporting his daughter's autonomy through paradox, framing the choice as an impossible double bind that exposes the absurdity of the pressure placed on Elizabeth. The pronouncement—'An unhappy alternative is before you, Elizabeth. From this day you must be a stranger to one of your parents'—is at once comic and genuinely protective.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
From this day you must
be a stranger to one of your parents.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The contrast between Jane's mild retreat from interference and Elizabeth's spirited resistance highlights Austen's exploration of different modes of feminine strength. Jane's gentleness and Elizabeth's wit represent complementary strategies for navigating a society that devalues women's choices. The narrator captures this duality precisely: Jane, with all possible mildness, declined interfering; and Elizabeth, sometimes with real earnestness, and sometimes with playful gaiety, replied to her attacks.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
She endeavoured to secure Jane in
her interest, but Jane, with all possible mildness, declined
interfering; and Elizabeth, sometimes with real earnestness, and
sometimes with playful gaiety, replied to her attacks.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Lydia's characterization as the eavesdropping, gossip-hungry sister introduces comic relief while foreshadowing her later indiscretions. Her whispered announcement of the 'fun' to Charlotte Lucas transforms domestic crisis into entertainment, revealing the performative nature of social scandal. The scene is crystallized in her greeting: she was met in the vestibule by Lydia, who, flying to her, cried in a half whisper, 'I am glad you are come, for there is such fun here!'
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
She was met in the vestibule by Lydia, who, flying to
her, cried in a half whisper, “I am glad you are come, for there is such
fun here!

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mrs. Bennet's theatrical self-pity—claiming exclusive suffering while dismissing others' perspectives—exemplifies Austen's critique of sensibility culture gone awry. Her declaration that 'those who do not complain are never pitied' ironically indicts her own manipulative deployment of emotion, since she does nothing but complain. The daughters' silent endurance is the only rational response: her daughters listened in silence to this effusion, sensible that any attempt to reason with or soothe her would only increase the irritation.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Her daughters listened in silence to this effusion, sensible that any
attempt to reason with or soothe her would only increase the irritation.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Collins's final speech, with its formal withdrawal and paradoxical resignation, showcases Austen's mastery of mock-heroic style. His elaborate justification—claiming he withdraws to avoid burdening the family with intercession—preserves his dignity through self-serving rhetorical flourishes while revealing his complete lack of genuine feeling for Elizabeth. The speech culminates in a characteristic blend of wounded pride and hollow magnanimity: 'My object has been to secure an amiable companion for myself, with due consideration for the advantage of all your family; and if my manner has been at all reprehensible, I here beg leave to apologize.'
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
My object has been to secure an amiable companion for myself, with due
consideration for the advantage of all your family; and if my _manner_
has been at all reprehensible, I here beg leave to apologize.

summary: Chapter XX of Pride and Prejudice centers on the fallout from Elizabeth Bennet's rejection of Mr. Collins's marriage proposal. The chapter explores themes of female agency versus economic necessity, parental authority, and the social performance of courtship. Mr. Collins's self-delusion, Mrs. Bennet's mercenary panic, and Mr. Bennet's ironic defense of his daughter create a rich satirical tapestry. Character interactions reveal the pressures facing young women in marriage negotiations while maintaining Austen's characteristic wit and psychological acuity.
